title: The hypertrophy series: mechanical vs muscular fatigue
summary: NH distinguishes muscular failure from mechanical failure: the stabilising structure (e.g. thoracic extension) gives out before the target muscles, shifting load onto joints and tendons. He argues this wastes tonnage and causes injury, and avoids it via rep-range selection per lift, reps in reserve, never grinding ugly reps, retaking sets, and strengthening weak links.

claims.claim: Most failed lifts are not muscular failure but mechanical failure: the muscle could keep pushing but the structure stabilising the weight loses integrity.

Examples of mechanical failure: upper back rounding in a back squat so you good-morning the weight up; hips shooting up in a deadlift so you lift with a rounded lower back like a crane. It can happen on bench, curls and every lift.
Mechanical failure is bad first because the tonnage stops going to the target muscle you want to grow.
Worse, under mechanical failure much of the tonnage goes onto skeleton and tendons rather than muscles; tendons don't need you to shift compound loads onto them, they grow fine with proper form.
Mechanical failure with near-maximal weight is the most likely path to injury, which is the great destroyer of tonnage because it stops you training.
NH believes deadlifts shouldn't be done in high rep ranges: hamstrings and glutes stay fresh while thoracic extension gives out first, raising injury risk and failing to challenge the muscles.
In front squats many people have far more leg strength than thoracic extension strength, so the upper back fails while the legs could keep going.
Avoiding mechanical failure starts with knowing your body, being humble, not ego lifting and not grinding through reps you know you shouldn't.

Use intensity and volume manipulation per lift: if a rep range pushes you into mechanical failure on a lift, avoid that rep range. For people who good-morning squats at low reps, squat in higher rep ranges.
The uncertain 'extra rep' is beneficial for mental strength and pushes muscles to the brink.
In higher rep sets the intensity jump between reps is smaller (rep 6 to 7 of 10 vs rep 2 to 3 of 3), so you can foresee the hard rep coming and stop before mechanical failure.
Leaving a rep in the tank costs much less of the set's tonnage at 10 reps than at low reps, where each rep represents a large share of the set.
Keep reps in the tank, especially on strength work, and aim to never have ugly reps; never allowing yourself to grind early reps prevents mechanical failure.
If you got the reps but the technique was ugly, retake the set next time. Tightening form so all tonnage hits the target muscles counts as progressive overload even without adding weight.
Mechanical failure often stems from specific weak links (thoracic extension, setup, technique) that can be strengthened or improved.
Accumulated mechanical fatigue causes overuse injuries like tendonitis: repeating a movement with weak technique makes skeleton and tendons take over from muscles until they give out.
